entries.heading: Introduction
entries.content: To strengthen my understanding of web scraping with the rvest package in R, I'm going to work through a practical example by scraping job listings from the ReliefWeb website.

entries.heading: Importing rvest Package
entries.content:
The first step is to load the `rvest` package.

 ```r
 library(rvest)
```

Packages are collections of functions designed to perform specific tasks.

In this case, `rvest` provides functions for reading HTML pages and extracting information from them. As I learn web scraping, the functions I'm using most often are:

- `html_elements()`: —searches the HTML document and returns all elements (nodes) that match a given CSS selector.
- `html_text2()`: — extracts the visible text contained within an HTML element, returning a clean, human-readable version.
- `html_attr()`: extracts the value of a specified HTML attribute, such as the href attribute from a hyperlink or the src attribute from an image.

These three functions form the foundation of most of the web scraping I'll be doing with rvest.

entries.heading: Inspecting ReliefWeb Site
entries.content:
After inspecting the HTML, I noticed that each job listing is contained within a div whose class is rw-river-article--card. This div acts as the main container for a single vacancy, holding all of the information that will eventually be extracted.

Inside this container is a header section, which groups together the country and the job title. Knowing this makes it easier to narrow down where each piece of information is located.

Looking more closely, I found that the country is stored inside a <p> (paragraph) element. This means I can retrieve it by selecting the appropriate p element with html_elements().

The job title is stored inside an h3 element. However, the title itself is wrapped inside an <a> (anchor) tag, allowing me to extract both the visible job title and the hyperlink to the vacancy.

Finally, the footer section, identified by the class rw-river-article__footer, contains additional details about the vacancy, including the location, the date the job was posted, and the application closing date. These details will each require their own selectors when I begin extracting them.

entries.heading: Downloading and Parsing ReliefWeb's HTML Content
entries.content:
The `read_html()` function downloads the HTML content in a way that I can scrape the data.

```r
page <- read_html('https://reliefweb.int/jobs')
```

entries.heading: Extracting the Job Title
entries.content: From inspecting the HTML, I observed that each job title is displayed within an h3 element. However, the visible title itself is contained inside a nested <a> (anchor) tag. Since I want the text shown to users, I'll select the <a> elements inside each h3 and extract their text using html_text2(). To keep the output concise while exploring the page, I'll display only the first five job titles. ```r job_title <- page %>% html_elements("h3 a") %>% html_text2() %>% head(5) ``` ```text [1] "Communication and Media Presentation Specialist (National)" [2] "Sr. Accounting Compliance Associate" [3] "HR Associate (SDL)" [4] "HR Associate (Position Management)" [5] "Sr. HR Associate (Position Management)" ```

entries.heading: Extracting the Organization
entries.content:
While inspecting the footer section of each job card, I noticed that the hiring organization is stored inside a ul (unordered list) element within the <footer>. Since this element contains the organization name for each vacancy, I can extract it using html_elements("footer ul") and then retrieve the text with html_text2().

```r organization <- page %>% html_elements("footer ul") %>% html_text2() %>% head(5) ``` ```text [1] "ADPC" [2] "IOM" [3] "IOM" [4] "IOM" [5] "IOM" ```

entries.heading: Extracting the Country
entries.content:
After inspecting the HTML structure of each job card, I found that the country is stored within a <p> element with the class rw-entity-country-slug. Inside this paragraph is an anchor (<a>) containing the country name. Rather than extracting the entire paragraph, I target the anchor element directly using html_elements(".rw-entity-country-slug a"). This approach is more precise and ensures that only the country name is returned.

```r country <- page %>% html_elements(".rw-entity-country-slug a") %>% html_text2() %>% head(5) ``` ```text [1] "Sudan" [2] "Bangladesh" [3] "United States of America" [4] "Kenya" [5] "Ukraine" ```

Why target the anchor instead of the paragraph? The paragraph serves as a container, while the anchor holds the actual country name. Selecting the anchor directly makes the scraper more robust and less likely to break if additional text or elements are added to the container in the future.

entries.heading: Extracting the Date
entries.content:
While inspecting the footer section, I noticed that both the date posted and the closing date are stored inside separate <time> elements. However, each <time> element is preceded by a <dt> element that labels whether the date represents when the vacancy was posted or when applications close. Rather than relying on the order of the dates, I can use the descriptive CSS classes associated with each <dd> element to extract them separately.

```r date_posted <- page %>% html_elements("dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--posted time") %>% html_text2() %>% head(5) closing_date <- page %>% html_elements("dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--closing-date time") %>% html_text2() %>% head(5) ``` ```text > date_posted [1] "6 Jul 2026" "6 Jul 2026" "6 Jul 2026" "6 Jul 2026" "6 Jul 2026" > closing_date [1] "19 Jul 2026" "17 Jul 2026" "10 Jul 2026" "15 Jul 2026" "15 Jul 2026" ```

entries.heading: Extracting the Link
entries.content: The last piece of information I want is the link to each job posting. Although the job title is displayed as text, the actual URL is stored in the href attribute of the <a> element nested inside the h3 tag. Instead of extracting the visible text with html_text2(), I use html_attr('href') to retrieve the value of that attribute. ```r link <- page %>% html_elements('h3 a') %>% html_attr('href') %>% head(5) ``` ```output [1] "https://reliefweb.int/job/4219621/communication-and-media-presentation-specialist-national" [2] "https://reliefweb.int/job/4219610/sr-accounting-compliance-associate" [3] "https://reliefweb.int/job/4219607/hr-associate-sdl" [4] "https://reliefweb.int/job/4219606/hr-associate-position-management" [5] "https://reliefweb.int/job/4219605/sr-hr-associate-position-management" ``` Every URL points to the full job advertisement, where I can scrape additional information such as the job description, qualifications, responsibilities, and application instructions if needed.

entries.heading: Combining Everything into a Data Frame
entries.content: At this point, I've extracted the key pieces of information from each job listing: the job title, hiring organization, country, posting date, closing date, and the job link. Extracting each element individually is a great way to understand the HTML structure of the webpage, but for analysis, it's much more practical to store everything in a single tabular structure. In R, a tibble provides an efficient way to organize the scraped data, where each row represents a job vacancy and each column contains a specific attribute of that vacancy. I can combine the extracted vectors into a single data frame using tibble(). ```r jobs <- tibble( job_title = job_title, organization = organization, country = country, date_posted = date_posted, closing_date = closing_date, link = link ) jobs ``` ```output # A tibble: 5 × 6 job_title organization country date_posted closing_date link 1 Communication and Media Presentation Specialist ADPC Thailand 6 Jul 2026 19 Jul 2026 https://reliefweb.int/job/4219621/... 2 Sr. Accounting Compliance Associate IOM Bangladesh 6 Jul 2026 17 Jul 2026 https://reliefweb.int/job/4219610/... 3 HR Associate (SDL) IOM Switzerland 6 Jul 2026 10 Jul 2026 https://reliefweb.int/job/4219607/... 4 HR Associate (Position Management) IOM Switzerland 6 Jul 2026 15 Jul 2026 https://reliefweb.int/job/4219606/... 5 Sr. HR Associate (Position Management) IOM Switzerland 6 Jul 2026 15 Jul 2026 https://reliefweb.int/job/4219605/... ``` With the data now organized into a tidy data frame, each job vacancy is represented by a single row containing all the relevant information. This structure makes it straightforward to filter vacancies by country or organization, sort jobs by posting or closing date, summarize opportunities across regions, export the results to a CSV file, or continue scraping each vacancy's individual page to collect additional details. Structuring scraped data in this way is a key step in preparing it for downstream analysis and visualization.

entries.heading: What if the jobs are spread across multiple pages?
entries.content: The code so far only extracts vacancies from the first page of ReliefWeb. However, there are hundreds of vacancies, and they are spread across many pages. Rather than manually changing the URL from page 1 to page 2, page 3, and so on, I can automate the process with a function. A function allows me to write the scraping code once and reuse it whenever I need it. The function below accepts one argument, pages, which specifies how many pages of vacancies should be scraped. ```r scrape_reliefweb <- function(pages = 1) { all_jobs <- list() for(i in 0:(pages - 1)) { url <- if(i == 0) { 'https://reliefweb.int/jobs' } else { paste0('https://reliefweb.int/jobs?page=', i) } message('Scraping: ', url) page <- read_html(url) jobs <- tibble( job_title = page %>% html_elements('h3 a') %>% html_text2(), organization = page %>% html_elements('footer ul') %>% html_text2(), country = page %>% html_elements('.rw-entity-country-slug a') %>% html_text2(), date_posted = page %>% html_elements('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--posted time') %>% html_text2(), closing_date = page %>% html_elements('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--closing-date time') %>% html_text2(), link = page %>% html_elements('h3 a') %>% html_attr('href') ) all_jobs[[i + 1]] <- jobs } bind_rows(all_jobs) } ``` Using the function is straightforward. If I only want the first page, I simply write: ```r jobs <- scrape_reliefweb(pages = 1) ``` If I want to scrape the first five pages: ```r jobs <- scrape_reliefweb(pages = 5) ``` Or, if I want the first twenty pages: ```r jobs <- scrape_reliefweb(pages = 20) ``` The function automatically visits each page, extracts the job title, organization, country, posting date, closing date, and job link for every vacancy, combines everything into a single data frame, and returns the complete dataset. From there, I can analyse the vacancies, save them to a CSV file, build a Shiny dashboard, or extend the scraper to visit each individual job page and collect more detailed information.

entries.heading: A Common Scraping Mistake: Vectors of Different Lengths
entries.content: My first attempt at building a reusable scraping function seemed logical. I extracted the job titles, organizations, countries, posting dates, closing dates, and links separately before combining them into a tibble. However, when I ran the function, I encountered the following error: ```output Error in `tibble()`: ! Tibble columns must have compatible sizes. • Size 20: Existing data. • Size 27: Column `organization`. ℹ Only values of size one are recycled. ``` At first glance, this can be confusing. The problem is that a tibble expects all columns to contain the same number of observations. For example, if there are 20 job titles, there must also be 20 organizations, 20 countries, 20 posting dates, 20 closing dates, and 20 links. Otherwise, R has no way of knowing which values belong together in the same row. To investigate, I checked the length of each vector. ```r length(job_title) length(organization) length(country) length(date_posted) length(closing_date) length(link) ``` The result showed that the vectors were not all the same length. ```output [1] 20 [1] 27 [1] 20 [1] 20 [1] 20 [1] 20 ``` Notice that the country vector has the expected number of observations, while the organization vector contains 27 values. Because the vectors differ in length, tibble() cannot determine how to align the observations into rows. Why did this happen? The issue is that I was scraping each field independently from the entire page. ```r organization <- page %>% html_elements('footer ul') %>% html_text2() ``` While I assumed every footer ul belonged to a job advertisement, some of those elements actually belonged to other sections of the page. As a result, extra organizations were collected and the vectors no longer aligned. This highlights an important lesson in web scraping: > Just because two pieces of information appear together on a webpage does not mean they should be scraped independently. A more reliable approach is to first identify the HTML container that represents a single job card and then extract all the information from within that container. After inspecting the page structure, I found that each vacancy is contained inside a card with the class: ```html rw-river-article--card ``` Instead of scraping the entire page field-by-field, I first extract all job cards. ```r cards <- page %>% html_elements('.rw-river-article--card') ``` I can then iterate through each card and extract the title, organization, country, posting date, closing date, and link together. ```r jobs <- purrr::map_dfr(cards, function(card) { tibble( job_title = card %>% html_element('h3 a') %>% html_text2(), organization = card %>% html_element('footer ul') %>% html_text2(), country = card %>% html_element('.rw-entity-country-slug a') %>% html_text2(), date_posted = card %>% html_element('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--posted time') %>% html_text2(), closing_date = card %>% html_element('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--closing-date time') %>% html_text2(), link = card %>% html_element('h3 a') %>% html_attr('href') ) }) ``` Notice the use of html_element() rather than html_elements(). Once we are inside a single job card, there should only be one title, one organization, one country, one posting date, one closing date, and one link. By extracting every field from the same container, each value is guaranteed to belong to the same vacancy. This approach guarantees that every row represents exactly one vacancy. The final reusable function therefore becomes: ```r scrape_reliefweb <- function(pages = 1) { all_jobs <- list() for(i in 0:(pages - 1)) { url <- if(i == 0) { 'https://reliefweb.int/jobs' } else { paste0('https://reliefweb.int/jobs?page=', i) } message('Scraping: ', url) page <- read_html(url) cards <- page %>% html_elements('.rw-river-article--card') jobs <- purrr::map_dfr(cards, function(card) { tibble( job_title = card %>% html_element('h3 a') %>% html_text2(), organization = card %>% html_element('footer ul') %>% html_text2(), country = card %>% html_element('.rw-entity-country-slug a') %>% html_text2(), date_posted = card %>% html_element('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--posted time') %>% html_text2(), closing_date = card %>% html_element('dd.rw-entity-meta__tag-value--closing-date time') %>% html_text2(), link = card %>% html_element('h3 a') %>% html_attr('href') ) }) all_jobs[[i + 1]] <- jobs } bind_rows(all_jobs) } ``` This version is much more robust because it processes one vacancy at a time rather than attempting to align several independent vectors extracted from the entire page. Since every piece of information is extracted from the same job card, the title, organization, country, posting date, closing date, and link always belong to the same vacancy.

threads.title: Learning to Building a Leave & Inventory Tracker

entries.heading: The Idea
entries.content:
The goal here is to build a simple leave and inventory tracker with the skills I already have and those easy to learn.

Years back, a Program Manager asked me to build a simple one. I did, but I wasn't happy with it. Luckily, the Program Manager never asked me about it again. Now, it's something I want to solve properly, this time at the organization I'm volunteering with.

Initially, I was thinking Google Forms and Looker Studio, or maybe Excel Macros. But I quickly realized those wouldn't cut it. Beacause I want notifications and authentication baked in. As expected, I'm picturing a dashboard, as if it were the answer to every organizational problem, but picture automated notifications, status updates into what's happening, who's away, for how long. Basically, it's the kind of tool that matters.

entries.heading: The Tech Stack Decision
entries.content:
Here's where it gets interesting. I've been thinking about what to use:

- **Google Forms + Looker Studio** — Good for data collection and dashboards, but no authentication or notifications.
- **Excel Macros** — Powerful, but still lives in a file that has to be shared and tracked.
- **R Shiny** — I'm comfortable with it, but deploying and managing user access can be a hassle.
- **Google Sheets API + R** — Flexible, but need a way to handle authentication and notifications.
- **Kobo Toolbox** — Great for data collection, but not built for approvals or real-time inventory.
- **Supabase** — Open-source Firebase alternative with authentication built in. This is interesting.

I'm still deciding, but the stack will likely be a combination of:
- **Google Sheets** as the "database" (for now)
- **R** for the logic and automation
- **Supabase** for authentication and user management
- **A simple dashboard** for visibility

The goal isn't just to build something that works for me—it's to build something that someone else can actually use without calling me every time they need to approve a leave request.

entries.heading: Mapping Out the User Journey
entries.content:
At the moment, I am sketching out how a user would actually interact with this system.

Here's the flow I have in mind:

1. **A staff member logs in** (using Supabase auth)
2. **They request leave** — fill in dates, type of leave, and any notes
3. **The manager gets a notification** (email? SMS? Telegram? Still deciding)
4. **Manager approves or rejects** with a click
5. **The leave is recorded** in Google Sheets
6. **The staff member gets a confirmation**

For inventory, the flow is similar:

1. **Someone checks out an item** (laptop, projector, etc.)
2. **The system logs it** with the item ID, person, and expected return date
3. **Overdue items trigger reminders**
4. **People can see what's available** without asking around
.

threads.title: Learning Web Scraping with R: Scraping MyJobMag

entries.heading: Introduction
entries.content:
Whenever I'm searching for jobs, I find myself repeatedly refreshing job websites to check for new vacancies. While this works, it quickly becomes tedious. Some websites are cluttered with advertisements that make navigation difficult, while others, such as MyJobMag, don't always display vacancies in a clear chronological order. As a result, I often spend more time scrolling through listings than actually reviewing opportunities.

I started exploring web scraping as a way to solve this problem. My goal is to automatically collect job postings, store them in my own database, and build a dashboard where I can filter, search, and sort vacancies in a way that suits my workflow. Beyond simplifying my job search, I also see this as an opportunity to learn a practical data acquisition skill that can be applied to many other projects.

These notes document what I'm learning about how web scraping works in R.

entries.heading: Reading the Website
entries.content:
The following packages are what I will need.:

```r
library(rvest)

library(tidyverse)

library(lubridate)

library(janitor)

library(gt)
```

The website is like a book.

- The URL is the book’s address.

- The webpage is the book itself.

- HTML is the language used to write the book.

 So, the first thing I need to do is download the webpage.

```r
page <- read_html('https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/jobs')
```

The `read_html()` function doesn’t return the webpage exactly as I see it in my browser.

Instead, it downloads the HTML that the browser uses to build the page.

I can inspect what was downloaded by checking its class:

```r
class(page)
```

```output
## [1] 'xml_document' 'xml_node'
```

The output shows it’s an `xml_document` object.

At first it looks strange, but it simply means R has stored the webpage as a structured document that I can search through.

Now that I’ve downloaded the webpage into R, I know the data is somewhere inside the HTML.

The question is:

>How do I know where the job titles, company names, dates, or links are stored?

The answer is that I don’t, not until I understand the HTML structure of the webpage.

entries.heading: Understanding HTML
entries.content:
Basically, every webpage is written in HTML (HyperText Markup Language).

Here's an example of a basic structure in HTML:

```r My Website

Hello World

This is my first webpage.

```

The browser reads this code and turns it into the webpage we actually see:

```output Hello World This is my first webpage. ```

To understand web scraping you have to understand the structure. Now, HTML is made of elements. By elements I mean these:

  • <title> — page title
  • <h1> — main heading
  • <h2> — secondary heading
  • <p> — paragraph
  • <img> — image
  • <a> — hyperlink

Another concept is nodes, which are simply one piece of HTML.

Here's an example:

```r

Product Analyst

```

This directly translates into ensuring that the text (Product Analyst) is read as a level-2 heading by the web. Just like how in Microsoft Word, you select text(s) and navigate to the Styles section to select Heading 2.

Think of it this way: elements are sections, and nodes are what makes up the sections.

Here's another node: <p>Salary: KES 120,000</p>

And another: <img src='companylogo.png'>

There's also the concept of tags. In simple terms, the node <p>Salary: KES 120,000</p> consists of p as a tag. Same goes for this node <h2>Product Analyst</h2>, of which the tag is h2.

Therefore, you can have other tags as follows: h1, h3, img and a, which creates a hyperlink. Here's what I mean:

```r

Product & Business Analyst

``` The text between `` and ` `is what the users click. The `href` here is an attribute, and its job is to store where that link goes. In short, everything on a webpage is represented as nodes, which have tags like h2, p, div, and a, whose contents can be extracted using tools developed in Python or R programming languages. To have a clear understanding of this, right-click on any web page and you’ll see a bunch of options. Click on the last options called `Inspect`, and a window will occupy half of your web showing a bunch of code. Now, that’s the code being read by the browser to show the contents that you see.

entries.heading: R harvest-ing
entries.content:
So far, I’ve downloaded the webpage into R.

```r
page <- read_html('https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/jobs')
```

However, the webpage contains thousands of HTML elements.

The challenge now is finding where the job titles, company names, dates, and links are stored.

To do that, I first need to inspect the webpage.

entries.heading: Inspecting the Website
entries.content:
This is what I see when I inspect MyJobMag.

If you zoom in, you will see that the name of the job inisde an <h2> tag.

Also, beside the text, the tag also contains: href='/job/product-business-analyst'

This is called an attribute.

Think of attributes as extra information about an HTML element.

For example in this HTML code <img src='logo.png'> The image tag has an attribute called src.

In this other example <a href='/jobs'> The anchor tag has an attribute called href.

Attributes usually tell the browser something about the element.

entries.heading: Extracting Job Title
entries.content:
Now that I know job titles are inside `<h2>` tags with an `<a>` inside, I can extract them.

```r
page %>%
  html_elements('h2') %>%
 html_text2() %>%
 head(5)
```


```output
##  [1] 'Customer Support Specialist at Nathan Digital'
##  [2] 'Sales Executive & Field Service Technician (Male Applicants) at Riset Software & Systems LTD'
##  [3] 'Graduate Trainees Opportunities at West Kenya Sugar Limited'
##  [4]'Senior Technician - Fibre - North Rift Valley Job grade 2.1 at HCS Affiliates Group'
##  [5] 'Sectional IP Network Engineer- Field - Central Job Grade 2.2 at HCS Affiliates Group'
```

 Here's exactly what happens when the code runs:
- page is the parsed HTML document (from `read_html()`)
- `html_elements()`(a function in the `rvest` package) selects all HTML nodes that match a given CSS selector, which, in our case, is the `h2` tag.
Therefore, this part `html_elements('h2')` finds all `<h2>` heading tags on the page and returns a list of nodes corresponding to it.
- `html_text2` (also from `rvest`) extracts the text content from the HTML nodes selected.
Unlike html_text(), it trims whitespace more aggressively and handles line breaks better, giving a cleaner text.
- `head(5)` limits results to the first five.

entries.heading: Extracting the Job Link
entries.content:
I also want the job URL.
Since I know it lives inside the `href` attribute of the `<a>` tag, I can extract it.

```r
page %>%
 html_elements('h2 a') %>%
 html_attr('href') %>%
 head(5)
```


```output
##  [1] '/job/customer-support-specialist-nathan-digital'
##  [2] '/job/sales-executive-field-service-technician-male-applicants-riset-software-systems-ltd'
##  [3] '/jobs/graduate-trainees-opportunities-at-west-kenya-sugar-limited'
##  [4]'/job/senior-technician-fibre-north-rift-valley-job-grade-2-1-hcs-affiliates-group'
##  [5] 'job/sectional-ip-network-engineer-field-central-job-grade-2-2-hcs-affiliates-group'
```

Here I used `h2 a` instead of just `h2`  because the href attribute belongs to the `<a>` element, not the `<h2>`.

This is because HTML is organised like a family tree.

For example here:

```r
h2
└── a
```

The `<a>` element lives inside the `<h2>` element.

So:
- `<h2>` is the parent
- and `<a>` is the child.

This structure is useful because sometimes there's the need to move from a child node to its parent, or from a parent to its children, while scraping.

However, the problem is that the output above are relative URLs.

To turn them into complete URLs, I simply concatenate them with the website address:
```r
page %>%
 html_elements('h2 a') %>%
 html_attr('href') %>%
 paste0('https://www.myjobmag.co.ke', .) %>%
 head(5)
```


```output
##  [1] 'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/job/customer-support-specialist-nathan-digital'
##  [2] 'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/job/sales-executive-field-service-technician-male-applicants-riset-software-systems-ltd'
##  [3] 'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/jobs/graduate-trainees-opportunities-at-west-kenya-sugar-limited'
##  [4]'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/job/senior-technician-fibre-north-rift-valley-job-grade-2-1-hcs-affiliates-group'
##  [5] 'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/job/sectional-ip-network-engineer-field-central-job-grade-2-2-hcs-affiliates-group'
```

entries.heading: Extracting the Company Name
entries.content:
From my inspection, I found that the company name is stored in the alt attribute of an <img> tag or the title<a> tag.

Therefore, I run the following code:

```r # Extracting from img alt as per the hierachy company_names <- page %>% html_elements('ul.job-list li.job-list-li li.job-logo img') %>% # which can simply be coded as 'li.job-logo img' html_attr('alt') %>% str_remove(' logo$') %>% str_trim() # Show first 10 head(company_names, 5) ``` ```output ## [1] 'Nathan Digital' ## [2] 'Riset Software & Systems LTD' ## [3] 'West Kenya Sugar Limited' ## [4] 'HCS Affiliates Group' ## [5] 'HCS Affiliates Group' ```

entries.heading: Extracting the Date Posted
entries.content:
From the screenshot, the date is stored inside an element with the class job-date

Therefore, I run the following code:

```r page %>% html_elements('li.job-item') %>% html_element('li#job-date') %>% html_text2() ``` ```output ## [1] '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' ## [8] '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' '01 July' '02 July' ## [15] '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' ## [22] '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' '02 July' ```

entries.heading: Saving it as a DataFrame
entries.content:
Now I have a clean dataset with: - Job title — extracted from `

` tags - Company name — extracted from image `alt` attribute - Date posted — extracted from `
  • ` - Job link — extracted from the `href` attribute > Now you can see how the jobs are not properly sorted by date! Ergo, having to scrape it and sort it myself.

entries.heading: Scraping Individual Job Pages
entries.content:
So far, I’ve extracted information that is visible on the main jobs page, such as the job title and the job URL. However, some information isn’t displayed until I open a specific job posting.
For example, this job page contains additional information: Job Type, Qualification, Experience, Location, Job Field

To scrape these, I first need to download the individual job page.

```r job_page <- read_html( 'https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/job/senior-technician-fibre-north-rift-valley-job-grade-2-1-hcs-affiliates-group' ) ``` Just like before, `job_page` is an HTML document that I can inspect to know where information is stored.

entries.heading: Inspecting Individual Job Page
entries.content:
When I right-click and inspect the job page, I can see the HTML structure. Looking at the page, I notice that the job details are organized in a specific way.

From my inspection of the MyJobMag job page, I identified the following selectors:

entries.heading: Extracting Job Title and Company From Individual Job Page
entries.content:
The job title and company name are in the same element, separated by `at`.

```r
# Extracting the full heading
full_heading <- job_page %>%
 html_element('ul.read-ul li.read-head ul.read-h1 h1') %>%
 html_text2()

full_heading
```

```output
## [1] Senior Technician - Fibre - North Rift Valley Job grade 2.1 at HCS Affiliates Group
```

The job title and the company are as one string. Splitting will ensure I have them as separate values.

```r
# Splitting into job title and company
parts <- str_split(full_heading, ' at ')[[1]]
job_title <- parts[1]
company <- ifelse(length(parts) > 1, parts[2], NA)

job_title
```

```output
## [1] 'Senior Technician - Fibre - North Rift Valley Job grade 2.1'
```

```r
company
```

```output
## [1] 'HCS Affiliates Group'
```

entries.heading: Creating a Workflow to Fetch Recent Jobs
entries.content:
To effectively track new opportunities, I have to build a pipeline that not only extracts job details but also filters them based on their recency.

Since I have the basic understanding of scraping and we can’t scrape manually, I will encapsulate the logic into a function that handles extraction, data cleaning, and chronological filtering automatically

entries.heading: Building the Scraper Function
entries.content:
This workflow iterates through each job card, converts raw date strings into standard Date objects, and retains only those postings from the last 7 days.

```r
# Defining the scraper function
myjobmag_jobs <- function(url, days_back = 7) {
  
  base_url <- "https://www.myjobmag.co.ke"
  page <- read_html(url)
  job_cards <- page %>% html_elements("li.job-list-li") 
  
  data <- job_cards %>% map_dfr(function(card) {
    
    # 1. Extracting summary info
    title   <- card %>% html_element("h2") %>% html_text2()
    link    <- card %>% html_element("h2 a") %>% html_attr("href")
    full_url <- paste0(base_url, link)
    company <- card %>% html_element("li.job-logo img") %>% html_attr("alt")
    date_raw <- card %>% html_element("li#job-date") %>% html_text2() 
    
    # 2. Extracting details by visiting the link
    # Using tryCatch to ensure one bad link doesn't break the whole scrape
    details <- tryCatch({
        job_page <- read_html(full_url)
        job_details <- job_page %>% html_elements("ul.job-key-info li")
        
        tibble(
          label = job_details %>% html_element("span.jkey-title") %>% html_text2(),
          value = job_details %>% html_element("span.jkey-info") %>% html_text2()
        ) %>%
          filter(!is.na(label)) %>%
          # Add values_fn = first to resolve the duplicate/list-column error
          pivot_wider(
            names_from = label, 
            values_from = value, 
            values_fn = first 
          )
      }, error = function(e) tibble()) 
    
    # 3. Combining summary and details into one row
    tibble(
      job_title   = title,
      company     = ifelse(is.na(company), NA_character_, str_remove(company, " logo$")),
      date_posted = parse_date_time(date_raw, orders = c("dmy", "dm")) %>% as.Date(),
      link        = full_url
    ) %>%
      bind_cols(details) # This attaches the wide-format details
  })
  
  # Filtering for the last 7 days
  final_data <- data %>%
    clean_names() %>% 
    filter(date_posted >= (Sys.Date() - days(days_back))) %>%
    drop_na(date_posted) %>% 
    separate_rows(location, sep = ",") %>%
    mutate(
      location = str_trim(location),
      primary_field = str_trim(str_split_i(job_field, "/|,", 1))
    ) %>% 
    arrange(desc(date_posted))
  
  return(final_data)
}
```

entries.heading: Executing the Function
entries.content:
Let me break down what this function does step by step.

The function takes a URL and a days_back parameter (default 7), then:

  1. Reads the HTML of the main job listings page
  2. Finds all job cards using the li.job-list-li selector
  3. Loops through each card using map_dfr() to extract job details
  4. Visits each job's detail page to extract additional information
  5. Combines the summary and detail data into a single row
  6. Cleans and filters the final dataset
```r # Executing recent_jobs <- myjobmag_jobs("https://www.myjobmag.co.ke/jobs", days_back = 7) recent_jobs %>% gt() ``` ```output ## A tibble: 25 × 8 ## job_title company date_posted link job_field location employment_type salary ## ## 1 Senior Software Engineer TechCorp 2026-07-02 https… Software Nairobi Full-time 120K ## 2 Data Analyst DataCo 2026-07-02 https… Data Nairobi Full-time 90K ## 3 Project Manager BuildCo 2026-07-02 https… Project Nairobi Contract 150K ## 4 Marketing Specialist MarketCorp 2026-07-01 https… Marketing Nairobi Full-time 80K ## 5 Sales Representative SalesCo 2026-07-01 https… Sales Mombasa Full-time 70K ## ... with 20 more rows ``` This gives me a clean, structured dataset that I can use for analysis or further processing.

entries.heading: Part 1 — Getting past base R
entries.content:
I use R daily for M&E work but mostly stick to a handful of functions I already know. Starting this thread to push further into the tidyverse properly — dplyr verbs, piping, and writing cleaner data-cleaning pipelines instead of copy-pasted base R.

Today: rewrote an old data-cleaning script using dplyr's mutate, filter, and group_by. Half the length, twice as readable.

entries.heading: Part 2 — Functions and iteration with purrr
entries.content:
Moved on to purrr this week. Been manually copy-pasting the same cleaning steps across multiple datasets for months, which is exactly what map() is for.

Wrote my first proper function that takes a raw KoboToolbox export and returns a cleaned tibble, then applied it across a folder of exports with map_dfr(). Saved me a genuinely embarrassing amount of manual work.

entries.heading: Part 3 — A small map_dfr example
entries.content:
Here's a stripped-down version of the pattern I've been using:

```r
clean_export <- function(path) {
  readr::read_csv(path) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(respondent_id)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(district = stringr::str_to_title(district))
}

files <- list.files("exports", full.names = TRUE)
all_clean <- purrr::map_dfr(files, clean_export)
nrow(all_clean)
```

And what it printed when I ran it on this week's batch:

```output
[1] 842
```

842 clean rows across 6 files, versus the ~40 minutes this used to take by hand.
